---
title: "Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function"
subtitle: "Systolic dysfunction, cardiogenic shock, and regional wall motion abnormalities"
---

## 1. Clinical question

*What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?*

::: {.callout-note}
**The bedside decision frame:** Two questions in order.

1. **Is global LV systolic function normal, reduced, or hyperdynamic?** A visual estimate of ejection fraction — severely reduced, mildly-to-moderately reduced, normal, or hyperdynamic — is sufficient for bedside decision-making. You do not need a number.
2. **Are there regional wall motion abnormalities?** Segmental dysfunction in a coronary distribution suggests ACS as the etiology. Global dysfunction is more consistent with cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, or sepsis-mediated depression. The distinction changes management immediately.
:::

Bedside LV assessment asks whether systolic dysfunction may be contributing to impaired perfusion. **EF is not cardiac output or a shock diagnosis.** A low EF may coexist with adequate output and vasodilatory shock; a small hyperdynamic LV may still eject a low stroke volume. Integrate perfusion, forward flow when measurable, RV findings, congestion, and a dynamic assessment of fluid responsiveness. Treatment follows the physiological problem, not the EF category alone.

---

## 2. Image acquisition

*Probe, windows, and technique for this module.*

Use a **phased array (cardiac) probe** on the **cardiac preset**. LV function is assessed across multiple windows — no single view is sufficient. The goal is to visualize the LV in two orthogonal planes and assess wall motion in all segments.

---

### Parasternal long axis

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Normal Parasternal Long Axis (PLAX) View.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Normal PLAX for LV assessment"/>
:::

**What you are looking for:** Global LV contractility (do the walls move vigorously inward in systole?), chamber size (a dilated LV suggests chronicity), and mitral valve excursion (reduced in low-output states). M-mode at the tips of the mitral valve leaflets allows measurement of EPSS (E-point septal separation) — a distance greater than 7 mm suggests reduced EF; greater than 13 mm correlates with severely reduced EF.

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Abnormal EPSS M-mode.png" style="max-width:100%;" alt="Abnormal EPSS on M-mode — increased distance between the anterior mitral leaflet E-point and the interventricular septum"/>
:::

---

### Parasternal short axis — papillary muscle level

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Normal Parasternal Short Axis View.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Normal PSAX at papillary muscle level"/>
:::

**What you are looking for:** The LV should appear round in cross-section and contract concentrically and symmetrically. This is the best single view for a visual EF estimate — watch the endocardium sweep inward in systole. Also assess the interventricular septum: a flat or D-shaped LV indicates RV pressure or volume overload (see Module 3).

---

### Apical four-chamber

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/apical+4+normal.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Normal apical four-chamber — wall motion reference"/>
:::

**What you are looking for:** All four chambers, with attention to LV wall motion in each visible segment. The apical view is essential for identifying apical wall motion abnormalities (LAD territory) and for assessing LV size relative to the RV.

---

### Subcostal

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/normal subcostal view.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Normal subcostal cardiac view"/>
:::

**When to use:** First-line in the unstable patient who cannot be repositioned. Provides a rapid visual impression of global LV function. Not sufficient alone for wall motion analysis.

---

## 3. Visual global assessment

*Train your eye by comparing the spectrum of LV function side by side. Use the normal clips as your reference, then scroll through progressively reduced function.*

---

### Normal LV function (EF 55–70%)

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Normal Parasternal Short Axis View.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Normal LV function on parasternal short axis"/>

<img src="gifs/apical+4+normal.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Normal LV function on apical four-chamber"/>
:::

Assess inward endocardial motion and systolic myocardial thickening across adequate views. Normal contraction reduces cavity size without requiring near-obliteration. If image quality or interpretation is uncertain, obtain additional views or expert/comprehensive assessment and document the limitation; uncertainty does not establish normal function.

---

### Hyperdynamic LV (EF >70%)

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/hyperdynamic short axis.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Hyperdynamic LV on short axis — near-complete cavity obliteration"/>
:::

Near-complete cavity obliteration in systole. Common in sepsis (early), anemia, hyperthyroidism, and hypovolemia. In a hypotensive patient, a hyperdynamic LV points away from cardiogenic shock — consider distributive or hypovolemic etiologies, though mixed shock states are possible.

---

### Mildly to moderately reduced LV (EF 30–54%)

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/moderately reduced EF short axis.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Mildly to moderately reduced EF on short axis"/>

<img src="gifs/moderately reduced EF apical 4 chamber.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Mildly to moderately reduced EF on apical four-chamber"/>
:::

Wall motion is reduced but clearly present. The LV may or may not be dilated. Does not automatically mean cardiogenic shock — assess for hemodynamic compromise and end-organ perfusion. Common in known heart failure presenting with decompensation. Treat the precipitant: arrhythmia, ischemia, infection, medication non-compliance. Avoid negative inotropes and large fluid boluses.

---

### Severely reduced LV (EF <30%)

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Reduced Ejection Fraction (Parasternal Long Axis View).gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Severely reduced EF on PLAX"/>

<img src="gifs/Decreased EF (Parasternal Short).gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Severely reduced EF on parasternal short axis"/>

<img src="gifs/Severe Depressed LV A4c.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Severely depressed LV on apical four-chamber"/>
:::

Wall motion and systolic thickening are globally reduced. The LV may be dilated, and EPSS may be increased. Severe dysfunction in a hypotensive patient warrants urgent assessment of perfusion and forward flow, but does not prove that cardiogenic shock is the dominant mechanism. Causes include ischemic or dilated cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, Takotsubo, and sepsis-associated dysfunction. Avoid empiric large fluid loads when congestion is present. Use vasoactive support or mechanical support according to the hemodynamic syndrome and specialist assessment, not EF alone.

---

## 4. Regional wall motion abnormalities

*Regional myocardial function is assessed by wall thickening and endocardial motion. Segmental dysfunction confined to a coronary territory suggests acute coronary syndrome — the pattern tells you which vessel is involved.*

---

### Coronary perfusion territories

<img src="images/coronary perfusion territories PSAX.png" style="max-width:400px; width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Coronary perfusion territories on parasternal short axis — LAD, RCA, and LCx distributions"/>

The LV is divided into segments that correspond to the three major coronary arteries. On the parasternal short axis at mid-papillary level:

- **LAD** (left anterior descending) — anterior wall, anteroseptal wall, apex
- **RCA** (right coronary artery) — inferior wall, inferoseptal wall
- **LCx** (left circumflex) — lateral wall, inferolateral wall, anterolateral wall

Recognizing which segments are affected tells you which vessel is the culprit — and whether the RV is at risk (RCA territory).

---

### Wall motion scoring

Each segment is graded by wall thickening in systole compared to diastole:

| Grade | Motion | Wall thickening |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | Normal endocardial inward motion | >40% increase |
| Hypokinetic | Reduced inward motion | 10–40% increase |
| Akinetic | Absent motion | <10% increase |
| Dyskinetic | Paradoxical outward motion in systole | Thinning or no thickening |

For focused cardiac ultrasound, the goal is to identify major abnormalities — severely hypokinetic, akinetic, or dyskinetic segments — not to formally score every segment.

---

### Anterior wall (LAD territory)

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/anterior wall hypokinesia short axis.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Anterior wall hypokinesia on parasternal short axis — LAD territory"/>
:::

Anterior and anteroseptal hypokinesis or akinesis on PSAX. On A4C, the apical and septal segments are affected. LAD occlusion produces the largest territory of dysfunction and is the most common cause of cardiogenic shock from acute MI.

---

### Inferior wall (RCA territory)

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Inferior and Lateral wall kypokinesis Psx - Case 1 Hypotension after STEMI.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Inferior and lateral wall hypokinesis on parasternal short axis — RCA territory"/>
:::

Inferior and inferoseptal dysfunction often involves the RCA territory, with variation by coronary anatomy. Assess the RV when inferior RWMA is present. In hypotensive RV infarction, assess preload and congestion before a cautious fluid challenge; reassess immediately and stop if flow or perfusion fails to improve or congestion worsens. Avoid preload-reducing drugs when hypotension or preload dependence is present. Urgent reperfusion remains central.

---

### Lateral wall (LCx territory)

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Lateral wall dyskinesia Psx - Case 3 Chest pain and new ECG changes.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Lateral wall dyskinesia on parasternal short axis — LCx territory"/>
:::

Anterolateral and inferolateral wall dysfunction on PSAX. On A4C, the lateral wall segments are affected. LCx territory infarcts are often ECG-silent (no ST elevation in standard leads) — bedside echo may be the first clue.

---

### Septal dyskinesis

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Septal Dyskinesis (Subcostal View).gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Septal dyskinesis on subcostal view"/>
:::

Paradoxical septal motion — the septum moves away from the LV cavity in systole instead of toward it. Can be seen after cardiac surgery (post-pericardiotomy), with a left bundle branch block, or with RV pressure overload causing septal shift. Not always ischemic — correlate with the clinical context.

---

### Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy on Apical Two Chamber View.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Takotsubo cardiomyopathy — apical ballooning on two-chamber view"/>
:::

Apical and mid-ventricular dysfunction with preserved basal contraction can suggest Takotsubo, especially when the distribution extends beyond a single coronary territory. Basal sparing alone does not distinguish it from distal LAD ischemia, and other Takotsubo patterns exist. Evaluate ACS appropriately rather than excluding it from the echo pattern. Stress history is supportive, not diagnostic. Recovery is common, but acute complications, including shock, require assessment. [International consensus](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5991205/).

---

## 5. Integration cases

*Cases where the finding changes management.*

---

### Case 1: Hypotension after STEMI

**Clinical scenario:** A 61-year-old man with an anterior STEMI is brought to the ED. He received aspirin and heparin in the field. On arrival his BP is 78/50, HR 110, and he is cool and diaphoretic. The cath lab team is being activated.

**What exam would you perform?**
Rapid focused cardiac ultrasound before transfer to the cath lab.

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/anterior wall hypokinesia short axis.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Anterior wall hypokinesia on parasternal short axis — Case 1, anterior STEMI"/>
:::

**What you see:**
Severely reduced EF. Anterior and apical wall akinesis. LV not markedly dilated (acute presentation). No pericardial effusion.

**How does this change management?**
The supplied STEMI and hypoperfusion make MI-related cardiogenic shock a major concern. Expedite coronary reperfusion and activate the shock team. Support arterial pressure and, if low output persists, consider inotropic support according to hemodynamics. Avoid large empiric fluid boluses. Mechanical support is selected case by case; it is not an automatic consequence of low EF. Do not delay transfer for a prolonged echo.

---

### Case 2: Undifferentiated hypotension in the ICU

**Clinical scenario:** A 58-year-old woman with septic shock from a urinary source has been on norepinephrine for 18 hours. She received 4 L of crystalloid. Her BP is now 72/40 despite escalating vasopressors. Lactate is rising.

**What exam would you perform?**
Bedside cardiac ultrasound — LV function, RV size, IVC.

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Severe Depressed LV A4c - Case 2 Undifferentiated hypotension in the ICU.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Severely depressed LV on apical four-chamber — Case 2"/>

<img src="gifs/Severe Depressed LV Psx - Case 2 Undifferentiated hypotension in the ICU.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Severely depressed LV on parasternal short axis — Case 2"/>

<img src="gifs/plethoric IVC - Case 2 Undifferentiated hypotension in the ICU.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Plethoric IVC — Case 2"/>
:::

**What you see:**
Severely reduced EF. Global hypokinesis. LV not dilated. IVC is plethoric.

**How does this change management?**
Sepsis-associated myocardial dysfunction may be contributing, but low EF and a plethoric IVC do not establish the dominant shock mechanism. BP 72/40 gives an approximate MAP of 51 mm Hg: continue resuscitation and titrate necessary vasopressor support. Pause further empiric fluid loading while assessing responsiveness and tolerance. Assess forward flow, perfusion, and congestion; obtain comprehensive echo and consider advanced hemodynamic monitoring if uncertainty persists. Inotropes may be appropriate for cardiac dysfunction with persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate volume and arterial pressure, in addition to required vasopressors. Reassess the response promptly after each intervention; a later repeat echo can follow myocardial recovery. [SSC 2026](https://www.sccm.org/survivingsepsiscampaign/guidelines-and-resources/surviving-sepsis-campaign-adult-guidelines).

---

### Case 3: Chest pain and new ECG changes

**Clinical scenario:** A 49-year-old woman presents with 2 hours of substernal chest pressure and diaphoresis. ECG shows ST depression in V4–V6. She is hemodynamically stable.

**What exam would you perform?**
Focused cardiac ultrasound to assess for RWMA.

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Lateral wall dyskinesia Psx - Case 3 Chest pain and new ECG changes.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Lateral wall dyskinesia on parasternal short axis — Case 3"/>
:::

**What you see:**
Lateral wall hypokinesis. Preserved global function. No effusion.

**How does this change management?**
This is suspected high-risk NSTE-ACS. A lateral RWMA supports the concern but may be old and does not alone establish acute infarction. Obtain serial ECGs and high-sensitivity troponin, begin appropriate ACS care, and involve cardiology urgently for risk-based invasive evaluation. Immediate angiography is indicated for qualifying very-high-risk features such as refractory/recurrent ischemia despite treatment, hemodynamic instability, or life-threatening arrhythmia; if present, do not wait for troponin. The stable scenario as written does not establish those features. [ESC ACS guideline](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191).

---

### Case 4: Young patient with viral prodrome and shock

**Clinical scenario:** A 28-year-old man presents with 5 days of viral URI symptoms followed by 24 hours of progressive dyspnea and now hypotension (BP 88/60). He has no cardiac history.

**What exam would you perform?**
Focused cardiac ultrasound.

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Case 4 Young patient with viral prodrome and shock.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Severely reduced EF with small pericardial effusion — myocarditis, Case 4"/>
:::

**What you see:**
Severely reduced EF. Globally hypokinetic but not dilated LV. No RWMA pattern. Small pericardial effusion.

**How does this change management?**
Suspected fulminant myocarditis with shock. The viral prodrome, global dysfunction, and small effusion support this working diagnosis but do not exclude ACS or other causes. Urgently involve cardiology/the shock team, stabilize pressure and perfusion, and consider mechanical support if needed. CMR can characterize inflammation when feasible; endomyocardial biopsy may be indicated in high-risk or unstable disease when the histological diagnosis changes treatment. Neither diagnostic test should delay resuscitation. [ESC 2025](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/46/40/3952/8234483).

::: {.callout-tip}
**Case format reminder:** The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis.
:::

## Quiz

::: {.callout-note}
**Q1.** A hypotensive patient has a hyperdynamic LV on bedside echo. What does this tell you about the etiology of shock?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
A hyperdynamic appearance makes severe global systolic depression unlikely, but does not establish adequate cardiac output or select a treatment. Consider distributive, hypovolemic, obstructive, and mixed mechanisms; assess stroke volume/forward flow, perfusion, and the rest of the examination. A small LV can eject a high fraction of a small end-diastolic volume.
:::

**Q2.** What is EPSS, and what does an elevated value indicate?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
E-point septal separation — the distance between the anterior mitral leaflet at its maximum opening excursion (E-point) and the interventricular septum, measured by M-mode on PLAX. Normal is less than 7 mm. Values above 7 mm correlate with reduced EF. It is a useful single-number surrogate when visual estimation is uncertain.
:::

**Q3.** You see hypokinesis of the inferior wall and posterior wall on PSAX. What coronary territory does this implicate, and what additional structure should you assess?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
Inferior and inferoseptal dysfunction often involves the RCA territory, with variation by coronary anatomy. Assess the RV when inferior RWMA is present. In hypotensive RV infarction, assess preload and congestion before a cautious fluid challenge; reassess immediately and stop if flow or perfusion fails to improve or congestion worsens. Avoid preload-reducing drugs when hypotension or preload dependence is present. Urgent reperfusion remains central.
:::

**Q4.** A patient has a severely reduced EF with a markedly dilated LV. A second patient has a severely reduced EF with a normal-sized LV. What does the difference in LV size suggest?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
LV dilation supports chronic remodeling such as dilated cardiomyopathy or longstanding ischemic disease, but it does not exclude a new acute insult. A nondilated LV with severe dysfunction raises concern for an acute process such as myocarditis, Takotsubo, or acute MI, but size alone cannot date the dysfunction. Compare prior imaging and integrate the presentation, ECG, biomarkers, perfusion, and a comprehensive examination.
:::

**Q5.** What is the Takotsubo pattern, and how does it differ from an LAD occlusion on bedside echo?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
A circumferential mid/apical pattern extending beyond one coronary territory raises suspicion for Takotsubo. Basal sparing alone is insufficient: distal LAD occlusion can spare basal myocardium. Integrate the acute presentation, ECG and biomarkers, and appropriate coronary evaluation to exclude ACS; do not diagnose Takotsubo from this pattern alone.
:::
:::

## References and further reading

- [ASE FoCUS recommendations](https://www.asecho.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/01/FCU.pdf): image limitations and nondiagnostic examinations.
- [SSC adult guidelines, 2026](https://www.sccm.org/survivingsepsiscampaign/guidelines-and-resources/surviving-sepsis-campaign-adult-guidelines): pressure support and inotrope indications.
- [Parker et al., 1984](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6703540/): depressed EF can coexist with normal/elevated cardiac index in septic shock.
- [RV infarction volume-loading study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0002914994903980): response depends on hemodynamics.
- [ESC ACS guideline, 2023](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191): risk-based invasive timing.
- [ESC myocarditis/pericarditis guideline, 2025](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/46/40/3952/8234483): CMR and biopsy pathways.
- [International Takotsubo consensus, Part II](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5991205/): differential diagnosis and coronary assessment.
